outcome: No event since 26 January 2024 has settled either the k-set question or the halving-line question, and neither gap between the best upper and lower bounds has closed. Three post-window events touch the named quantities: a 2024 refinement of the additive constant in the even-n upper bound on halving lines (Symmetry, Alonso, Lopez, Rodrigo), a 2024/2025 raising of the halving-line lower bound at four specific n = 35, 59, 95, 97 (Axioms, Rodrigo et al.), and a 2024 higher-dimensional halving-hyperplane bound for d >= 5 (Rubin, an analogue that does not address the plane).
problem_asks: (a) K-sets: matching upper and lower bounds on the maximum number of k-sets of a set of n points, as a function of n and k. (b) Halving lines: matching upper and lower bounds on the maximum number of halving lines of a set of n points. The statement gives no dimension. This record reads it as planar, because both quantities are planar in the source article's main statement and the statement names no higher dimension; higher-dimensional analogues are recorded as analogues where found. 'Matching' is not defined in the statement. This record reads it as the upper and lower bounds having the same asymptotic order, and leaves the tolerance to the judging pass.

events.what_happened: Estrella Alonso, Marilo Lopez and Javier Rodrigo, 'An Improvement of the Upper Bound for the Number of Halving Lines of Planar Sets', Symmetry 16(7):936. They improve the additive constant in the best known asymptotic upper bound on h_n, the maximum number of halving lines of n planar points with n even, and improve that upper bound explicitly for 106 <= n <= 336. The method bounds from below the sum of squared degrees of the halving-line graph (via Cauchy-Schwarz, then pattern analysis); per the search-result summary, the authors say a prior reference bounded only the principal term and left this error term unbounded. Known only from abstract-level and metadata search snippets; the article text could not be retrieved.
events.revisions: MDPI dates: submitted 31 May 2024; revised 10 July 2024; accepted 11 July 2024; published 22 July 2024. No arXiv or other preprint found, so the publication date is used as the first public appearance.
events.delivers: Restricted to the upper bound on h_n for even n. Improves the additive constant of the best asymptotic upper bound and gives improved explicit upper bounds for 106 <= n <= 336. The Wikipedia K-set article, read through a summarising fetch tool and not checked against the paper, states the even-n bound as h_n <= (29/8)^(1/3) * n * (n-1)^(1/3). Does not change the exponent 4/3 and says nothing about odd n, the lower bound on h_n, or k-sets.
events.remains: Matching asymptotics for halving lines: the upper bound is still of order n^(4/3) (only its constant moved) against the lower bound n * e^(Omega(sqrt(log n))). Odd n is untouched. Every part of the k-set question is untouched.

events.what_happened: Javier Rodrigo Hitos, Marilo Lopez, Danilo Magistrali and Estrella Alonso Perez, 'An Improvement of the Lower Bound on the Maximum Number of Halving Lines for Sets in the Plane with an Odd Number of Points'. Preprints.org 202411.1953, later Axioms 14(1):62. Explicit planar point sets raise the best known lower bound on h_n at n = 35, 59, 95 and 97, and the lower bound on halving pseudolines for n = 35 in the plane and projective plane. Per search-result summaries of the paper, the sets come from deleting two points from the best known sets for h37, h61, h97 and h99 (as listed on Aichholzer's rectilinear crossing page), using a recursive relation between h_n and h_(n+2) that the paper proves. The paper says the crossing-number upper bound for these n follows only if a conjecture of Abrego et al. on 3-symmetric optimal drawings holds. Known from metadata and abstract-level snippets; the full text could not be retrieved.

events.what_happened: Tamal Dey, 'Improved Bounds for Planar k-Sets and Related Problems'. Upper bound O(n (k+1)^(1/3)) on the maximum number of k-sets of n planar points, and O(n^(4/3)) on halving lines (the halving bound is attributed to Dey in every source read). The method uses the crossing-number inequality of Ajtai, Chvatal, Newborn and Szemeredi, building on Agarwal, Aronov and Sharir. Preliminary version at FOCS 1997, pp. 156-161; journal version Discrete and Computational Geometry 19 (1998) 373-382, DOI 10.1007/PL00009354.

events.what_happened: One manuscript in the family: “A power saving for planar halving lines” (OpenAI, dated September 25, 2026). Its Theorem 1 (thm:halving-power) says there are absolute constants ε>0, C and n0 such that every even n ≥ n0 and every n-point set in R² with no three collinear has h(P) ≤ C n^{4/3−ε} unordered halving pairs; since distinct pairs give distinct lines, this bounds halving lines too. This improves the classical O(n^{4/3}) halving-line bound that the introduction attributes to Dey (1998). The core is Theorem 2 (thm:all-ranks): for a generic N-point planar configuration and any rank k, the number of switches S_k(P) in a rank-k sweep is at most C N^{4/3−ε}, uniformly in k. The middle-rank case gives Theorem 1. Corollary 3 (cor:k-sensitive) is the k-set statement: for every n-point Q ⊂ R² with no three collinear and every 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2, the number of k-sets is at most C₀ n (k+1)^{1/3−ε₀}, with absolute ε₀ > 0 (the proof takes ε₀ = min{ε, 1/6}). The same bound is given for the complexity of a level in an arrangement of n non-vertical lines with no parallel pair and no three concurrent. Dey's bound for k-sets is O(n(k+1)^{1/3}) (stated in the manuscript's introduction), so the new result improves the exponent of (k+1) from 1/3 to 1/3−ε₀. At k near n/2 it gives about n^{4/3−ε₀}, the same order as the new halving bound. The proof is a finite reduction to exchange graphs and crossing counts, followed by a proof by contradiction that produces a uniform little-o improvement of a packing estimate. That improvement is taken from a limiting spatial measure of dimension 32/17, and a fixed-scale induction turns it into the power saving. The manuscript gives no lower-bound result of its own. It recalls the existing lower bounds for halving lines, Ω(n log n) from Erdős, Lovász, Simmons and Straus and n·exp(Ω(√log n)) from Tóth and Nivasch, and says they remain far below any fixed power n^{1+δ}.
events.delivers: For the upper-bound half of the problem, the claim establishes: (i) for planar halving lines, a bound of O(n^{4/3−ε}) for even n ≥ n0 with no three collinear, for an absolute but unspecified ε > 0; (ii) for planar k-sets, a bound of O(n(k+1)^{1/3−ε₀}) for all 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2 and no three collinear, for an absolute but unspecified ε₀ > 0; (iii) the same level-complexity bound for arrangements of complete straight lines (not pseudolines, not segments), which the manuscript says gives no corresponding saving for pseudolines or line segments. The constants and exponents are nonquantitative: no numerical value of ε, ε₀, C, C₀ or n0 is given. The results are planar only. Nothing in the manuscript is stated for dimensions above two. The claim is an upper bound only. It gives no lower bound for k-sets or for halving lines, and it does not show that the upper and lower bounds have the same order. The abstract and the theorems describe a power saving over O(n^{4/3}); the manuscripts do not claim to settle the problem, and their framing does not say the problem is solved.
events.remains: If the claim is correct, the following remain open. (a) Halving lines: the gap between the new upper bound n^{4/3−ε} and the known lower bounds of order n·exp(Ω(√log n)) (and the older Ω(n log n)) is not closed, and the manuscript itself says the lower bounds stay far below any fixed power n^{1+δ}. (b) K-sets: the manuscripts give no lower bound at all for the maximum number of k-sets as a function of n and k, so the matching-bounds question for part (a) of problem_asks is open in full. The k-dependence exponent 1/3−ε₀ is not claimed to be tight. (c) The value of the exponent is not determined, so even the upper bound is not explicit. (d) Dimensions above two, and pseudoline or segment settings, are not addressed.

machine_checked.scope: A halving pair in an even planar point set is a pair whose line leaves equally many remaining points on each side. The formalization proves that some absolute $\varepsilon>0$ and $C$ bound the number of halving pairs by $Cn^{4/3-\varepsilon}$ for every sufficiently large even $n$ and every $n$-point set with no three collinear. It also proves a bound of the same form for all level-switch counts under the additional generic-position assumptions in the statement. The constants are existential.

events.doubts: (1) The power saving depends on Theorem activity-packing, a little-o improvement of a packing estimate. Its proof is by contradiction (rank-limits.tex opens with 'suppose, for a contradiction'; boundary.tex closes it) and runs through rank coordinates, differentiability, a zoom lemma, a spatial measure, and a strip count. That chain is long and several links are stated in prose. The introduction says the conditional-measure and Lipschitz-differentiability statements are 'specified at their applications'. (2) The introduction calls the limit order 'crucial': limits are taken first at a fixed small rank scale and then far along the sequence of configurations. boundary.tex also says that restriction to G is done only after weak convergence, and that the limits along countably many windows come from diagonal subsequences. (3) finite.tex, eq. (finite-localized-crossing), keeps an additive 13824 S³ term, and the text says this term 'may only be discarded after an appropriate limiting normalization'. (4) Some proofs are only partly written out. The spatial proposition's proof begins with 'We first select a positive set' and relies on a metric input stated only as eq. (spatial-metric-input), with its own quantifiers. The zoom lemma is called elementary but its proof is long. (5) The k-set corollary's level-to-cell step is given in outline ('the cited shallow-cutting reduction now gives'). (6) The abstract, the introduction and Theorem 1 agree with each other. I found no inconsistency between the statements and the main theorems. The text says the constants are nonquantitative, which limits how far the bound can be checked numerically.; conditional on: No unproven hypothesis is assumed by the theorems. Some steps rely on cited external results that the manuscript does not reprove: the shallow-cutting lemma of Matoušek as stated by Agarwal, Aronov, Chan and Sharir (used for the level and k-set corollary, in recurrence.tex, where the cut-to-level step is stated as following from the cited reduction); and standard background cited in the introduction (Simon 2014 for differentiation of finite measures; Chabrillac and Crouzeix 1987 for monotone-function differentiability, which the text also proves in outline). The imbalanced crossing argument is attributed to Pach, Solymosi and Tardos, and the classical crossing lemma to Ajtai et al. and Leighton; the manuscript says it reproves the reduction and constants it needs. The chain-partition mechanism is stated to be the one underlying Dey (1998). No other OpenAI manuscript is cited or used.

disputes.summary: The Omega(n log k) lower bound on k-sets is credited to Erdos, Lovasz, Simmons and Strauss (1973) and independently to Edelsbrunner and Welzl (1985). Both are pre-window; recorded as independent events, not resolved.
Dey's planar k-set bound is dated 1997 (FOCS 1997 preliminary; Erickson's page) and 1998 (DCG 19; Wikipedia summary). Both are recorded in the Dey event.

Sources disagree on the direction of the Erdos et al. conjecture about h_n. One summary reads it as an upper bound, h_n = o(n^(1+eps)). Another search summary attributes an n^(1+eps) conjecture to a construction context, which may concern a different function. The primary 1973 text was not read, so this is unresolved.

summary: Searched across 44 queries (listed below) and about 35 page fetches, several of them blocked, covering the problem name and variants, the 2024-26 papers, the classical bounds, AI-specific announcements, and the lab and tracker sources. Nothing settled either part of the statement (the planar maximum number of k-sets; the planar maximum number of halving lines), and the best exponents are unchanged from their January 2024 values: upper bounds O(n (k+1)^(1/3)) (Dey, 1997/98) for k-sets and O(n^(4/3)) (Dey, 1998) for halving lines; lower bounds n * 2^(Omega(sqrt(log k))) (Toth, 1999/2001) and n * e^(Omega(sqrt(log n))) (Toth, with Nivasch's 2006 constant). Three post-window events concern the quantities the statement names; two more post-window items, a 2026 crossing-number paper on K33 and the OpenAI unit-distance result, are recorded as discounted events on neighbouring questions. (i) Alonso, Lopez and Rodrigo (Symmetry, published 22 July 2024) improve the additive constant of the upper bound on h_n for even n and give explicit improvements for 106 <= n <= 336. I could not read the article (MDPI returned 403, the PDF 410), so I cannot confirm the constant, which the Wikipedia article reports as (29/8)^(1/3) n (n-1)^(1/3). (ii) Rodrigo et al. (preprint 26 Nov 2024; Axioms, 16 Jan 2025) raise the lower bound on h_n at n = 35, 59, 95, 97 by deleting two points from the record sets for n = 37, 61, 97, 99. The crossing-number consequence depends on the Abrego et al. 3-symmetric conjecture. Full text not read. (iii) Rubin (arXiv 1 March 2024) improves higher-dimensional halving-hyperplane bounds for d >= 5. This is an analogue and does not address d = 2. Close calls. First, whether (i) and (ii) count as a quantity the statement names having moved. They move the constant of an upper bound and finitely many values of h_n, and they leave the asymptotic gap as it was. A reader who counts any moved value of h_n as progress would call the problem 'moved'; one who requires the asymptotic gap to close would call it unmoved. The record does not choose. Second, the dimension. I read the statement as planar, since both quantities are planar and the statement names no dimension. If the intended problem includes 3D k-sets and halving planes, the 3D events (Sharir-Smorodinsky-Tardos 2000; Aronov et al. 1990) and Rubin's d >= 5 result come into scope. None of them changed a 3D exponent in the window that I found, except possibly the undated 3D halving-plane log-factor refinement I could not read. AI. No source about a halving-line or k-set result names an AI system, and I found no AI-attributed result on this problem. The AI search covered: the OpenAI unit-distance result (May 2026; recorded as a discounted event on a different problem, with an unnamed 'internal OpenAI model' credited in a secondary quote, not the authors' own account); OpenAI's Astra list (1 August 2026; secondary coverage names ten results, none identified as k-sets or halving lines; primary post not opened); AlphaEvolve (arXiv 2511.02864; a full-text keyword check across three portions found no halving, k-set, or crossing-number terms, though it was done by a summarising fetch tool; section titles include Heilbronn, Erdos-Szekeres and equidistant-point problems, none on this topic); PatternBoost (arXiv 2411.00566; experiment list of nine problems, none on this topic); a Quanta article (3 August 2026; no mention of k-sets or halving lines); and Erdos-problem trackers (not reached, no k-set entry identified). Because the 2024 and 2025 MDPI papers were not read, none_found is true for them on the basis of their abstracts and metadata; this should be checked against the full text.
competing_reading: Read the Symmetry (2024) and Axioms (2025) papers as real movement in the named quantity h_n. The first sharpens an upper bound with explicit small-n values; the second raises lower bounds at four n. On this reading the problem has events in both directions and the 'nothing settled asymptotically' verdict is a judgement about 'matching', not about whether anything moved. Against that: neither changes an exponent, and the statement asks for matching bounds, so the asymptotic gap is the thing asked about. The Axioms gain is at four values of n; the Symmetry gain is a constant and a finite range. On the stricter reading, the problem is unmoved.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full texts of Symmetry 16(7):936 (doi 10.3390/sym16070936) and Axioms 14(1):62 (doi 10.3390/axioms14010062): the exact upper-bound constant, the new h(35), h(59), h(95), h(97) lower-bound values, and each paper's statement on computer search or AI tools. (2) Primary texts of Dey (FOCS 1997; DCG 1998) and of the Erdos-Lovasz-Simmons-Strauss 1973 paper, to settle the dates and the direction of the Erdos conjecture. (3) Nivasch's written paper, if one exists, for its date. (4) Aichholzer's rectilinear-crossing page, for the current h(n) records. (5) A 2025-2026 citation search for any planar k-set or halving upper bound beyond Dey's, and for any lower bound polynomial in k. (6) The OpenAI Astra primary post and its manuscripts, to confirm that none of the ten results concerns k-sets or halving lines. (7) The authors' acknowledgements in the 2024-25 MDPI papers, for AI or software use.

event.what_happened: Estrella Alonso, Marilo Lopez and Javier Rodrigo, 'An Improvement of the Upper Bound for the Number of Halving Lines of Planar Sets', Symmetry 16(7):936. They improve the additive constant in the best known asymptotic upper bound on h_n, the maximum number of halving lines of n planar points with n even, and improve that upper bound explicitly for 106 <= n <= 336. The method bounds from below the sum of squared degrees of the halving-line graph (via Cauchy-Schwarz, then pattern analysis); per the search-result summary, the authors say a prior reference bounded only the principal term and left this error term unbounded. Known only from abstract-level and metadata search snippets; the article text could not be retrieved.
event.revisions: MDPI dates: submitted 31 May 2024; revised 10 July 2024; accepted 11 July 2024; published 22 July 2024. No arXiv or other preprint found, so the publication date is used as the first public appearance.
event.delivers: Restricted to the upper bound on h_n for even n. Improves the additive constant of the best asymptotic upper bound and gives improved explicit upper bounds for 106 <= n <= 336. The Wikipedia K-set article, read through a summarising fetch tool and not checked against the paper, states the even-n bound as h_n <= (29/8)^(1/3) * n * (n-1)^(1/3). Does not change the exponent 4/3 and says nothing about odd n, the lower bound on h_n, or k-sets.
event.remains: Matching asymptotics for halving lines: the upper bound is still of order n^(4/3) (only its constant moved) against the lower bound n * e^(Omega(sqrt(log n))). Odd n is untouched. Every part of the k-set question is untouched.

events.credibility_reason: Would be the first exponent improvement over Dey's n^(4/3) since 1998; the key packing improvement rests on a long compactness/contradiction chain with several steps only partly written out (spatial proposition, zoom lemma, shallow-cutting step in outline), an additive 13824 S^3 term discarded only after a limiting normalisation, non-quantitative constants, Lean build with sorry_free unrecorded, and 8 days without expert reading. No specific error identified.

judgement.why: The statement asks for matching (same-order) upper and lower bounds for planar k-sets and halving lines; nothing in the record closes either gap. The OpenAI manuscript claims a power saving n^(4/3-ε) for halving lines and n(k+1)^(1/3-ε0) for k-sets — a genuine exponent move on both named quantities but with no lower bound, so it is a bound, unreviewed (Lean formalisation is not digestion, F7), doubtful given the length and partial write-up of the limiting argument, and AI-generated per the repository README, which attributes the results to the internal model. The Symmetry 2024 paper moves the additive constant of the even-n upper bound: a bound, accepted by a journal. The Axioms paper raises h_n at four specific n only, which is finitely many instances of an asymptotic question, so instances. Rubin (d>=5), the K33 crossing paper and the unit-distance result are different questions (variant). Pre-snapshot classical bounds are bounds; 3D, dense, random and algorithmic work are variants.
judgement.doubts: The OpenAI AI attribution rests on a repository-wide README sentence ('the vast majority of results'), not a per-paper statement; taken as generated since the repository presents the manuscripts as model output. The two MDPI papers were not read in full, so their AI/software use is unverified. Rodrigo 2024 could be argued as a bound (record lower values of h_n) rather than instances; chosen instances because it fixes finitely many n and leaves the asymptotic quantity untouched.
